opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, and it's one I come back to a lot because my work is on robot learning, so I'm constantly comparing how a robot learns a skill with how a person, or even an animal, learns one.

There are some deep similarities. Reinforcement learning, which is a big part of what we do in robotics, was originally inspired by how animals learn. You try something, you get a reward or a punishment, and over time you do more of what works. When we trained quadruped robots to walk in simulation, it looked a lot like a baby learning to walk. At first the robot falls over constantly, flails its legs, does all kinds of strange things. Then gradually it finds a gait that works. That trial-and-error process feels very familiar.

But I think the differences are more interesting, and they tell us where machine learning still has a long way to go.

The first is data efficiency. A child can see a cup once or twice and know what a cup is. They can watch an adult open a door once and try it themselves. Our robots often need millions of trials in simulation to learn something as basic as walking. We get around that with tricks like massively parallel simulation, running thousands of robots at the same time, much faster than real time. That's a capability humans don't have, so in a sense we're compensating for poor sample efficiency with brute force.

The second is prior knowledge. Humans don't start from scratch. Evolution has given us a body, reflexes, and a brain already structured to learn certain things. Babies have a basic sense of physics and objects very early. For a long time robots started from a blank slate, which is part of why learning was so slow. One of the most exciting changes in the last few years is that large foundation models, language models and vision-language models trained on internet-scale data, give robots something like common sense. With that, a robot can understand "pick up the thing you'd use to clean up this spill" without being trained on that exact instruction. It's not quite how humans acquire common sense, but it plays a similar role: a strong prior that makes learning new things much faster.

The third is embodiment. Humans learn through their bodies, through physical interaction with the world, from the very beginning. Language models learn mostly from text, which is a kind of second-hand record of human experience. I believe that to get truly general intelligence, at least the kind that can act in the physical world, you need that embodied loop of acting, seeing what happens, and adjusting. That's part of why I'm so passionate about robotics. It forces learning to be grounded in reality.

So my view is that human learning is still a great source of inspiration, but we shouldn't just copy it. Airplanes don't flap their wings. Machines have their own advantages, like perfect memory, the ability to share experience instantly across thousands of robots, and simulation. The best path is probably to borrow the key principles from human learning, like strong priors, curiosity, and learning from interaction, and combine them with what machines do uniquely well.

r001.rationale: The response compares trial-and-error learning and discusses foundation models trained on internet-scale data, but it does not identify distilling information from accumulated data as a similarity between human and machine learning.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because my work on legged robots is really sitting right at that boundary.

The first thing I'd say is that the two are more similar than people often assume, at least at the level of principle. When a child learns to walk, nobody hands them a manual. They try, they fall, they get some signal from the world about whether what they did worked, and they adjust. That's essentially reinforcement learning. Trial, feedback, update. So when we train a robot dog to walk in simulation, we're borrowing something very old from biology, not inventing something alien.

But the differences are where it gets interesting, and I think they're more instructive than the similarities.

The most obvious one is data efficiency. A human toddler learns to walk in maybe a year with a few thousand falls. Our robots need millions, sometimes billions of simulated steps to learn something comparable. And that gap tells you something. It tells you humans aren't learning from scratch. There's an enormous amount of prior structure already built in, from evolution, from the body itself, from the way our sensory systems are wired. Machine learning in its purest form starts with almost no prior. So a lot of what we do as researchers is actually trying to inject the kind of priors that biology got for free.

The second difference is transfer. A person who learns to walk on a sidewalk can walk on sand, on ice, up stairs, with surprisingly little extra effort. Our systems have historically been brittle. Change the friction coefficient a little and the policy collapses. Closing that gap, what we call sim-to-real and generalization, has been the central problem of my field for the past decade. And honestly, studying how humans do it has been one of our best sources of ideas. Humans adapt online. They use a rough internal model and correct it constantly. That shaped how we think about domain randomization and adaptive controllers.

The third thing, and this is more philosophical, is that human learning is embodied and purposeful in a way that's hard to replicate. A child doesn't learn to walk because someone defined a reward function. They want to reach the toy across the room. The locomotion is a means. In machine learning we still spend a huge amount of effort hand-designing rewards, and the reward is often the hardest part. So in some sense humans are solving a harder and more open-ended problem than our robots, and doing it with less supervision.

Now, I'd push back on the idea that it's a one-way street, where machines just try to imitate humans. Machine learning is also becoming a tool for understanding human learning. When we build a system and watch where it fails, that failure is a hypothesis about what biology must be doing differently. And there are areas where machines genuinely surpass us. A robot can learn in parallel across ten thousand simulated bodies at once. No human can do that. So the ideal isn't for machines to copy humans. It's to figure out which parts of biological learning are deep principles and which are accidents of hardware.

If I had to compress it into one sentence, I'd say human learning is the existence proof. It tells us that efficient, robust, general learning is possible in the physical world. Machine learning is our attempt to understand that proof well enough to write it down.

r001.rationale: The response compares learning through trial, feedback, and updating, but does not identify distilling information from accumulated data as a similarity.

astra-6.text:
I think human learning and machine learning are closely related, but they’re also quite different. Both involve learning from experience and using that experience to handle new situations. When we learn a skill, we try something, observe the result, and adjust. Reinforcement learning follows a similar pattern: an agent takes actions, receives feedback, and gradually improves its behavior.

But humans bring much more to the process. We use prior knowledge, learn from other people, and make connections across different experiences. If someone explains a new game to you, you can often start playing after a few sentences. A machine learning system may need many examples or attempts to learn the same behavior.

So I see human learning as a source of inspiration, rather than something machine learning has to reproduce exactly. Studying how people learn can help us build machines that learn more efficiently and generalize better. And trying to build those machines can also help us ask more precise questions about what learning actually involves.

r001.rationale: The response says both learn from experience, but does not identify distilling information from accumulated data as their similarity.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human learning and machine learning are closely related, but they’re not the same. Both involve learning from experience and using what we’ve learned to handle new situations. Machine learning gives us a mathematical way to describe some of that process: a system makes predictions, receives feedback, and adjusts.

But people bring much more to learning. We have physical experience, prior knowledge, curiosity, and social interaction. We can often learn something from just a few examples because we connect it to things we already understand. Machines can be very effective at learning patterns from large amounts of data, yet still struggle when the situation changes.

So I see the relationship as going in both directions. Human learning inspires ways to build better machines, and studying machine learning gives us ways to ask more precise questions about learning itself. But success in one doesn’t necessarily mean we fully understand the other.

r001.rationale: The response says both learn from experience and apply learning to new situations, but it does not identify distilling information from accumulated data as their similarity.
